concept.technique_name: clue-and-contrast word matching in a two-blank text completion

examples.problem_statement: While some feel that the author’s (i) _________ late in his life (ii) _________ his reputation, others felt that his dissolution added a certain glamour to his biography and credibility to his libertinous tales. Blank (i): vitiation / debauchment / deterioration. Blank (ii): derogated from / bedizened / aggrandized.

solution.operation: Locate the sentence's clue words: “dissolution” and “libertinous”
solution.result: The clue describes a life falling apart — drugs, promiscuity, crime, or general dissipation
solution.description: Read the second half of the sentence and pull out the words that describe the author's late-life conduct; these are the clue the blanks must agree with.

solution.operation: Match blank (i) to the meaning of “dissolution” / “libertinous”
solution.description: Choose for the first blank the option whose meaning is the same kind of moral dissipation the clue describes, since blank (i) simply names what “dissolution” refers to.

solution.operation: Read the contrast set up by “while some feel … others felt … added a certain glamour” to fix the charge of blank (ii)
solution.description: Because the “others” hold the positive view that the dissolution added glamour, the first group's view must be the opposite, so the word going into blank (ii) has to act negatively on his reputation.

solution.operation: Select the negative option among “derogated from,” “bedizened,” and “aggrandized”
solution.description: Apply the negative requirement from the previous step to the second blank's choices and keep the only one that means to detract from something.

key_reminders: The blank must agree with the sentence's own clue word; here “dissolution” and “libertinous” point to the same idea as the answer.
A “while some … others …” frame signals contrast: if one side's view is positive, the blank on the other side must be negative.
common_mistakes: Taking “deterioration” or “vitiation” for blank (i): both mean a general worsening or spoiling, but neither carries the specific moral dissipation that “dissolution” and “libertinous” signal.
Choosing “aggrandized” for blank (ii), which points the wrong way — it matches the “others” who saw glamour rather than the “some” whose view the blank expresses.

concept.technique_name: algebraic translation of a comparison into an inequality

examples.problem_statement: Translate the following statement into a mathematical relationship: Jean has more than twice as many CDs as Kim.

solution.operation: Let J = Jean's number of CDs and K = Kim's number of CDs
solution.result: J and K stand for the two counts being compared
solution.description: Give each person's CD count a letter so the sentence's comparison can be written symbolically.

solution.operation: Multiply Kim's number by 2 to represent “twice as many as Kim”
solution.description: Turn the phrase “twice as many CDs as Kim” into an expression by doubling the quantity that belongs to Kim.

solution.operation: Join J to 2K with an inequality sign rather than an equals sign: J > 2K
solution.description: Since the sentence says more than twice, not exactly twice, connect Jean's count to the doubled amount with a greater-than sign instead of equality.

key_reminders: “Twice as many as X” multiplies X itself by 2, so the doubling attaches to Kim's count, not Jean's.
“More than” makes the statement an inequality; only “exactly” or “as many as” would justify an equals sign.
common_mistakes: Writing 2J > K, doubling the wrong person because Jean is named first in the sentence.
Writing J = 2K, dropping the “more than” and turning a strict inequality into an equation.

concept.technique_name: sentence-equivalence selection by matching the sentence's implied reaction

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole: Because they had expected the spacecraft Voyager 2 to be able to gather data only about the planets Jupiter and Saturn, scientists were ______ the wealth of information it sent back from Neptune twelve years after leaving Earth. (A) anxious for (B) confident in (C) thrilled about (D) keen on (E) elated by (F) eager for

solution.operation: Note the words “expected” and “only” in the opening clause
solution.result: The data received exceeded what the scientists had expected
solution.description: Read the “Because” clause and see that the scientists had anticipated far less, so the information from Neptune was more than they had counted on.

solution.operation: State what the blank must therefore mean
solution.result: A reaction to results that are better than hoped for
solution.description: Convert the finding from the previous step into a requirement on the blank: it has to describe how one responds to an unexpectedly good outcome.

solution.operation: Test each choice against “reaction to better-than-hoped-for results”
solution.result: “thrilled about” and “elated by” both express such a reaction
solution.description: Check the options one at a time and keep the two that name delight at an outcome that surpassed expectation.

solution.result: Eagerness is not explained by the unexpectedness of the information
solution.description: Discard the two words that describe anticipation rather than response, since the sentence's causal “Because” clause gives no reason for the scientists to have been eager for data they never expected.

examples.answer: Choice C: thrilled about AND Choice E: elated by

key_reminders: A “Because” clause states the cause of the blank; the chosen words must be explained by that cause.
“Expected … only” signals that what actually happened went beyond expectation.
common_mistakes: Picking “eager for” and “keen on” as the pair — they form a plausible synonym pair, but they describe anticipation before the fact, which the unexpectedness in the sentence does not support.
Choosing “confident in” or “anxious for,” which contradict the scientists' stated low expectation of the Neptune data.
